common_name: Sadandy Southern Pea (Early Purple Hull Cream Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep once soil has warmed past 65°F and frost danger has passed; Sadandy is a fast, heat-tolerant Louisiana heirloom that can be succession sown every few weeks through midsummer for a continuous Gulf South harvest.

directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing seeds a few inches apart in rows and thinning if needed. Sadandy is a Louisiana heirloom purple hull-type southern pea prized for its unusually early maturity and heavy, concentrated fruit set on compact, bushy plants, letting gardeners get a full picking in one or two passes rather than the extended trickle typical of many purple hulls. Pods mature to a deep purple that shows clearly against the green foliage, signaling when the cream-colored peas inside are ready to shell, and the pods hold well without shattering even in Gulf Coast heat and humidity. Like other cowpeas its roots fix nitrogen, so it also serves well as a quick-turnaround soil-building crop between spring and fall vegetables. Harvest at the purple-pod stage for fresh shelling or let dry fully on the vine for storage peas.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Southern Pea Variety Trials
Mississippi State University Extension — Southern Pea Production Guide

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm soil after all frost danger has passed; Dixielee carries strong resistance to root-knot nematode and fusarium wilt, making it a dependable choice for southern gardens where those soilborne problems have limited other southern pea varieties.

directions: Direct sow in full sun into warm, well-drained soil, choosing this variety over other cream peas if root-knot nematode or fusarium wilt has been a problem in the bed. Dixielee was released by the University of Georgia specifically for its combined resistance to root-knot nematode, fusarium wilt, and southern pea mosaic virus, packaged into a productive, semi-vining plant that yields extra-large cream-colored peas with excellent fresh and canning quality. Pods are borne well above the foliage for easy picking and hold their quality over a longer harvest window than many older cream-type varieties. As with other cowpeas it fixes nitrogen in the soil, benefiting whatever crop follows. Harvest pods once they fill out and begin to yellow for fresh shelling, or leave to dry fully for storage.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Southern Pea Variety Recommendations
Mississippi State University Extension — Southern Pea Production Guide

common_name: Brown Crowder Southern Pea (Heirloom Drying Crowder Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; Brown Crowder is a vigorous, heat-loving heirloom that thrives through the hottest, most humid stretch of the Gulf South growing season.

directions: Direct sow in full sun in warm, well-drained soil, allowing extra room for the semi-vining growth habit to sprawl. Brown Crowder is a traditional Southern heirloom named for the way its brown-hulled peas pack tightly, or 'crowd,' against one another inside the pod, developing the rich, earthy flavor and quick-cooking texture prized in old-fashioned Southern pea dishes. Vigorous vines produce heavily even in the poor, sandy soils and intense heat that stall many other legumes, and the plants show good general tolerance to common cowpea pests and diseases. Like other cowpeas, Brown Crowder fixes nitrogen through its root nodules, leaving the soil enriched for a following crop. Pick pods green for fresh shelling once well filled, or let them dry fully on the vine for classic dried crowder peas.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension — Southern Pea Production Guide

common_name: Alyceclover (Warm-Season Forage and Cover Crop Legume)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill into warm, well-prepared soil after all frost danger has passed; alyceclover establishes slowly at first but grows vigorously once soil and air are warm, and it tolerates the wet, poorly drained, low-fertility soils common along the Gulf Coast better than most other summer legumes.

directions: Broadcast seed inoculated with the appropriate rhizobium at a shallow depth into a firm, warm seedbed in full sun; alyceclover is a warm-season annual legume long used across the Gulf South as summer forage, hay, and a nitrogen-fixing cover crop on soils too wet, acidic, or infertile for cowpeas or soybeans. It forms a dense, leafy, upright stand that suppresses weeds, tolerates close grazing or repeated mowing by regrowing from lower nodes, and fixes meaningful nitrogen for the crop that follows. Because it is frost-tender and slow to establish in cool soil, wait until soil has fully warmed before sowing, and expect a full, weed-suppressing stand within six to eight weeks under good moisture. Mow or graze before heavy frost, or terminate and incorporate the residue three to four weeks ahead of the next planting to let the nitrogen-rich foliage break down.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Alyceclover Plant Guide
